rationale: This is a single-knob smoothing variant of the already-tested archive winner rather than a new mechanism, and it quietly drops the `aqc` acquisition term from the investment denominator, so a change in performance will be confounded between smoothing and the narrower definition of "investment requirement."

Reduced to its economics this is rank(profitability) minus rank(asset growth) — a near-mechanical composite of the RMW and CMA legs already inside the FF5 benchmark plus the published asset-growth anomaly — so the diagnostic about operator structure is likely to be answered by factor absorption rather than by mispricing, and it re-tests the same channels as the archive signal.

Deflating both the earnings leg and the spending leg by the same installed-capital base is a genuinely coherent construction that measures harvesting versus capacity addition on a common scale, and industry ranking sensibly neutralizes the dominant capital-intensity confound; the main residual risk is partial overlap with the archive's margin-versus-capex divergence signal, which used the same two ratios in trend rather than level form.

The labor-margin channel is genuinely absent from the archive and the expression matches the stated hypothesis, though the reviewer should note that the hiring-rate leg is itself a published anomaly and that `emp` sparsity plus small/zero denominators may compress coverage and destabilize the productivity leg.

The second leg is essentially net external financing (debt issuance plus equity issuance scaled by assets), making the signal a direct rediscovery of the well-documented external-financing/net-issuance anomaly combined with a cash-flow profitability sort, with little incremental content beyond published results and the FF5 legs.

Recasting the winning coverage ratio as an own-history position poses a substantively different level-versus-transition hypothesis rather than a cosmetic tweak, but a 5-observation annual TS_RANK is a very coarse, discretized variable that will blunt cross-sectional dispersion and may mechanically weaken the Fama-MacBeth slope for reasons unrelated to the economics.
